666.title: Divine Mercy Sunday
666.hook: the second Sunday of Easter, named by John Paul II in 2000
666.howItsDone: On Divine Mercy Sunday many Catholic parishes display the Divine Mercy image, hear the Gospel of Thomas, offer confession, and pray the Divine Mercy chaplet, often at three in the afternoon; the words Jesus, I trust in you are printed beneath the image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Easter octave: eight days kept as one. Your line was one long day. What small Easter thing did you keep going? Today is the octave's last day. Day six hundred sixty-six.

In a convent in Poland in the 1930s, a young nun with little schooling kept a notebook. Her name was Faustina Kowalska. She wrote that Jesus had appeared to her, robed in white, with two rays streaming from his heart, one pale and one red. She was asked to have the image painted, with five words underneath. She died of tuberculosis in 1938, at thirty-three. Sixty-two years later, in Rome, a Polish pope declared her a saint, and gave a name to the Sunday that ends the Easter octave.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK IN A POLISH CONVENT.` → `TWO RAYS, PALE AND RED.` → `FIVE WORDS UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: On the thirtieth of April, 2000, John Paul II canonized Faustina and announced that, from then on, the second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday across the whole Church. The Latin word for mercy, misericordia, joins the heart, cor, to someone's misery. The readings didn't change. The Gospel this Sunday has always been John 20: the risen Jesus walking through locked doors, breathing on the disciples, and saying, in the Douay-Rheims, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." The very first thing he does with frightened friends who ran away is hand them the power to forgive. Then Thomas, who wasn't there, gets his own visit a week later, and Jesus says: "Blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." So the feast's theme was already sitting in the text. Faustina's image puts it in a picture: the two rays are often explained as the blood and water that flowed from his side. And the five words at the bottom, in her Polish, are the ones Catholics now pray: Jesus, I trust in you. A surprise: for about twenty years, the Vatican restricted this devotion, partly because of flawed copies of her writings. The restriction was lifted in 1978, the year a cardinal from Kraków, where she had lived, became pope. Catholics are free to take up Faustina's devotions or not; the Church approves them without requiring them. But the line itself is short enough for anyone to carry. Five words. Not I understand. Not I'm sure. Just trust.
screen: `NAMED ON 30 APRIL 2000.` · `THE GOSPEL: FORGIVE, AND THOMAS.` · `TWO RAYS: BLOOD AND WATER.` · `RESTRICTED, THEN LIFTED IN 1978.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT HAVE NOT SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: five words, slowly. Sit and let your breathing settle. Think of one thing you're carrying that you can't fix today. Name it. Then, if you pray, say Faustina's line on your breath: Jesus, I trust in you. Breathe in on Jesus, out on the rest. Let it repeat for as long as the bell holds. If you don't pray, simply hold the worry in an open hand instead of a fist. The bell holds the time.
Divine Mercy Sunday. The second Sunday of Easter, given that name by John Paul II in 2000, when he canonized Saint Faustina. Today's word.
Your line: Jesus, I trust in you. Today, when the worry you named comes back, say the five words once, or simply open your hand. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: Good Shepherd Sunday
667.hook: the fourth Sunday of Easter, a day of prayer for vocations
667.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Easter Catholic parishes hear a Gospel from John 10 about the Good Shepherd and keep the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, praying for priests and religious, often with a talk from a seminarian or sister.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Divine Mercy Sunday and Faustina's five words. Your line was Jesus, I trust in you. When the worry came back, what did you do with it? Day six hundred sixty-seven.

Somebody calls your name across a crowded airport. You turn before you've even thought about it. Not because the voice was loud, but because it was yours, and the person knew it. Two Sundays after the octave ends, on the fourth Sunday of Easter, every Catholic parish in the world hears a Gospel about exactly that: a shepherd whose sheep know his voice. And since 1964 the Church has made it a day of prayer about a call. Today's word is the Latin name for being called.
screen: `A NAME ACROSS AN AIRPORT.` → `THE FOURTH SUNDAY OF EASTER.` → `A DAY ABOUT A CALL.`

segments.voice: Every year on this Sunday the Gospel comes from John chapter ten, a different slice of it in each year of the three-year cycle. In one year, the gate of the sheepfold, and this line, in the Douay-Rheims: "the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." In another, I am the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep. In the third, my sheep hear my voice, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand. A shepherd in Jesus's world didn't drive his flock from behind with dogs. He walked ahead and called, and they followed the voice they knew. The word vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call. In 1964 Pope Paul VI began a World Day of Prayer for Vocations, and it settled on this Sunday. Most parishes pray especially for priests and for men and women entering religious life, and you'll often hear a seminarian or a sister speak at Mass. But the Church uses the word more widely than that. The Catechism speaks of a vocation to love that everyone has, and of marriage as a vocation too. A married couple, a single person caring for a parent, a nurse on night shifts: Catholic teaching says each of them can be answering a call. And the call in John isn't a job description first. It's a name. He calls his own by name, and then leads them out.
screen: `JOHN TEN, EVERY YEAR.` · `A SHEPHERD WALKS AHEAD AND CALLS.` · `VOCARE: TO CALL.` · `PRIESTS, SISTERS, MARRIAGE, EVERYONE.` · then, large: `HE CALLETH HIS OWN SHEEP BY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is discerning. Sit, and think of someone you know who is at a fork right now. Maybe a young person wondering about the priesthood or the convent. Maybe a friend deciding whether to marry, or to change careers, or to move home and care for someone. Picture their face. Say their name quietly. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply wish them clarity and courage. The bell holds the time.
Vocation. From the Latin vocare, to call. In Catholic teaching, a call from God, to priesthood, religious life, marriage, or a life of love in the world. Today's word.
Your line: he calls by name. Today, use people's names: the cashier, the coworker, the neighbor. Notice how they turn. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 667 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OUR LADY OF FATIMA (13 MAY).`

668.title: Our Lady of Fatima (13 May)
668.hook: three shepherd children in Portugal in 1917, asking for prayer and penance
668.howItsDone: On 13 May many Catholics pray the rosary for peace, and pilgrims gather at the shrine in Fatima, Portugal, for candlelight processions; the appearances are approved as worthy of belief, but Catholics are not required to believe in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Shepherd Sunday and the word vocation. Your line was he calls by name. Whose name did you say today that you usually skip? Day six hundred sixty-eight.

May 1917. Europe is three years into a war that has already killed millions, and Portugal has sent its own soldiers to the trenches. In the hills near a village called Fatima, three children are watching sheep: Lucia, ten, and her younger cousins Francisco and Jacinta, eight and seven. It's around noon on the thirteenth of the month. They later said that a flash like lightning came, and then a lady brighter than the sun, standing over a small oak tree. She asked them to come back on the thirteenth of every month. And she asked them to pray the rosary every day, for peace in the world and the end of the war.
screen: `MAY 1917: EUROPE AT WAR.` → `THREE CHILDREN WITH SHEEP.` → `PRAY THE ROSARY FOR PEACE.`

segments.voice: The children did come back, every month through October, and the crowds grew from a handful of neighbors to many thousands. On the thirteenth of October, in pouring rain, a huge crowd gathered, and many there, including reporters, described the sun seeming to spin and plunge. People still argue over what they saw. The message the children carried was simple and demanding: pray, especially the rosary; do penance; make sacrifices for sinners; pray for peace. Francisco and Jacinta took it so seriously that they offered up small hungers and discomforts, the way children would. Both died young, in the flu epidemic that followed the war, in 1919 and 1920. In 2017, a hundred years after the first appearance, Pope Francis canonized them at Fatima, among the youngest saints the Church has ever named who were not martyrs. Lucia became a nun and lived until 2005. Here's a point worth knowing. The Church judged the Fatima appearances worthy of belief in 1930, and popes have gone there on pilgrimage. But Catholic teaching calls these private revelations. They add nothing to the faith; the Church allows and encourages devotion to them, and does not require any Catholic to believe them. What Fatima asks for, though, is old: the rosary, and Mary as the one who points to her son. As she said in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "all generations shall call me blessed." Today, the thirteenth of May, many Catholics pray a decade for peace.
screen: `EVERY THIRTEENTH THROUGH OCTOBER.` · `PRAY, DO PENANCE, PRAY FOR PEACE.` · `TWO CHILDREN, SAINTS IN 2017.` · `WORTHY OF BELIEF, NOT REQUIRED.` · then, large: `ALL GENERATIONS SHALL CALL ME BLESSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a decade for peace. A decade of the rosary is one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and one Glory Be. If you pray, you can pray one now, on beads or on your fingers, for one place at war. Name the place first. If you don't pray, sit with the name of that place, and the children there, for the length of ten slow breaths, and then a few more. The bell holds the time.
Our Lady of Fatima. Mary as three Portuguese shepherd children described her in 1917, asking for prayer, penance and peace. Her day is the thirteenth of May. Today's word.
Your line: pray for peace. Today, when you see a headline about a war, stop for one breath and say the place's name. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: The Ascension
669.hook: forty days after Easter; in many places moved to Sunday
669.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension forty days after Easter, on a Thursday, or where bishops have transferred it, on the following Sunday; many then pray a novena to the Holy Spirit in the days before Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Fatima and three children in a world war. Your line was pray for peace. Which place did you name? Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Picture the last day of an apprenticeship. For years you've worked beside the master, watched his hands, handed him tools. Then one morning he gives you the keys, says the shop is yours, and walks out. You stand there holding the keys, staring at the door. That's roughly where the disciples are at the start of the Acts of the Apostles. Forty days after Easter, on a hill outside Jerusalem, they're staring at the sky. Two strangers in white have a question for them. Today, the Ascension.
screen: `THE KEYS TO THE SHOP.` → `FORTY DAYS AFTER EASTER.` → `STARING AT THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it twice, at the end of his Gospel and at the start of Acts. Acts says that for forty days after his passion Jesus showed himself alive and spoke of the kingdom of God. Then, on the Mount of Olives, he tells them they'll be his witnesses to the ends of the earth, and while they watch, he's lifted up and a cloud takes him out of their sight. And then the two men in white, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand you looking up to heaven?" It's almost funny. Stop looking up. There's work down here. Mark's Gospel ends the same way, with the apostles going out: "But they going forth preached every where: the Lord working withal." Catholics believe the Ascension is not Jesus leaving the world, but the risen Christ, body and all, entering the glory of the Father, and from there sending the Spirit. The forty days count from Easter Sunday, so the feast falls on a Thursday, Ascension Thursday. But in many countries, including most of the United States, the bishops have moved it to the following Sunday so that more people can keep it. Either way, it begins a short stretch of nine days before Pentecost: the disciples went back to the upper room with Mary and prayed together. That first nine days of prayer is where the Catholic custom of the novena comes from. The master has handed over the keys. The work is theirs now, and he promised not to leave them alone with it.
screen: `FORTY DAYS, THEN A CLOUD.` · `WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP?` · `THURSDAY, OR MOVED TO SUNDAY.` · `NINE DAYS OF PRAYER TO PENTECOST.` · then, large: `YE MEN OF GALILEE, WHY STAND YOU LOOKING UP TO HEAVEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up, then look around. If you can, go to a window or step outside. First, look up at the sky for a few breaths. Clouds, blue, gray, a ceiling if that's what you have. Then lower your eyes and look around you, slowly, at what's actually here: the street, the room, the people, the dishes in the sink. Ask one question: what here is mine to do? If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
The Ascension. Forty days after Easter, the risen Jesus taken up into heaven before the apostles' eyes. Kept on a Thursday, or in many places the following Sunday. Today's word.
Your line: the work is ours now. Today, do the one thing you noticed was yours to do, before you've finished wishing someone else would. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

670.title: Pentecost
670.hook: the golden sequence: come, father of the poor
670.howItsDone: On Pentecost Sunday Catholics wear red at Mass, hear the story of the Spirit's coming in Acts 2, and sing or recite the sequence Veni, Sancte Spiritus before the Gospel; the Easter season ends that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ascension, and the apostles staring at the sky. Your line was the work is ours now. What did you do that was yours to do? Day six hundred seventy.

Nine days in a locked room. The apostles, Mary, some of the women, praying and waiting. Jerusalem outside is packed with pilgrims for a harvest festival, the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover. Then, Acts says, a sound from heaven like a mighty wind fills the whole house, and something appears like tongues of fire, resting on each one of them. They spill out into the street speaking, and a crowd from a dozen countries hears them, each in their own language. Twelve hundred years later, someone wrote a song for this day that the Church still sings before the Gospel.
screen: `NINE DAYS IN A ROOM.` → `WIND, AND TONGUES OF FIRE.` → `A SONG FOR THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Pentecost comes from the Greek for fiftieth: fifty days after Easter, the way the Jewish feast of weeks falls fifty days after Passover. Acts describes it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "there appeared to them parted tongues as it were of fire." On this day the Mass has a sequence, an old poem sung after the second reading. There are only two sequences the Church requires all year, one at Easter and this one. It's called the golden sequence, and it's usually credited to Stephen Langton, an archbishop of Canterbury who died in 1228, though nobody can prove he wrote it. It opens in Latin: "Veni, Sancte Spiritus." Come, Holy Spirit. Then a run of lines, each one calling the Spirit by a new name. The first is "Veni, pater pauperum." Come, father of the poor. Then giver of gifts, light of hearts, best comforter, the soul's sweet guest. Later verses ask the Spirit to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is stiff, warm what is cold. Notice where it starts. Of all the names it could have used first, it chose the poor. Not the powerful, not the learned. In Acts, the Spirit fell on fishermen and a few women in a borrowed room, and the first thing the new community did, a few verses later, was share what they had so no one was in need. The sequence remembers that. The Spirit comes first to people who have nothing to bring.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `TONGUES AS IT WERE OF FIRE.` · `THE GOLDEN SEQUENCE.` · `IT STARTS WITH THE POOR.` · then, large: `VENI, PATER PAUPERUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: come, Holy Spirit. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one place in you that's dry, or cold, or stiff: a resentment, a tiredness, a door you've closed. Don't fix it. Just bring it to mind. If you pray, you can say the old opening words on your breath, in Latin or English: Veni, Sancte Spiritus. Come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, simply breathe in as if you were opening a window in that room. The bell holds the time.
Veni Sancte Spiritus. Latin for come, Holy Spirit: the opening of the golden sequence sung at Mass on Pentecost. Today's word.
Your line: come, father of the poor. Today, notice one person who has nothing to bring, and bring them something: time, a meal, your attention. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Trinity Sunday
671.hook: the Sunday after Pentecost is about who God is
671.howItsDone: On the Sunday after Pentecost Catholics celebrate Trinity Sunday, wearing white at Mass and professing the Creed; every day Catholics mark themselves with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost and the golden sequence, Veni Sancte Spiritus. Your line was come, father of the poor. Who had nothing to bring, and what did you bring them? Day six hundred seventy-one.

Most feasts remember something that happened: a birth, a death, a rising, a wind in a room. Trinity Sunday is different. Nothing happened on it. No event, no saint, no story. The week after Pentecost, having walked through the whole year of what God did, the Church stops and asks the question underneath all of it: who is God? A Catholic has been answering that question since before they could talk, every time an adult traced a cross over them. Today, the feast of that answer.
screen: `A FEAST WITH NO EVENT.` → `WHO IS GOD?` → `AN ANSWER TRACED ON YOUR BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's a surprise first: the word Trinity isn't in the Bible. What's there is a pattern. At the end of Matthew, the risen Jesus sends the apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice it says the name, singular, then three. Paul ends a letter to Corinth with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost. Early Christians found themselves praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and needed words for what they were already doing. Around the year 200, a writer in North Africa named Tertullian used the Latin trinitas, a threeness. The great councils of Nicaea and Constantinople in the three hundreds gave the Creed Catholics still say on Sunday. The Church's teaching is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, each fully God, not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks. The Church calls it a mystery, which in its language doesn't mean a puzzle to give up on. It means something true that you can keep going deeper into forever. The feast itself spread slowly through the Middle Ages, and in 1334 Pope John XXII put it on the calendar of the whole Church. There's a famous story that Saint Patrick explained the Trinity with a shamrock. It's lovely, and it's a later legend; his own writings don't mention it. What Catholics actually do every day is simpler. They touch forehead, chest and both shoulders, and say the name.
screen: `THE WORD ISN'T IN THE BIBLE.` · `TERTULLIAN: TRINITAS.` · `ONE GOD, THREE PERSONS.` · `A MYSTERY TO GO DEEPER INTO.` · then, large: `IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the sign of the cross, three times, slowly. Sit, and breathe. The first time, just do it, the way you've done it a thousand times, and notice how fast it usually goes. The second time, pause at each touch: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right shoulder. The third time, let each name take a whole breath. If you're not someone who makes the sign, simply sit and notice your breath going in, resting, going out. The bell holds the time.
Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, kept for the whole Church since 1334, on the mystery of one God in three persons. Today's word.
Your line: one god, three persons. Today, the next time you make the sign of the cross, or see someone make it, slow it down by one breath. Day six hundred seventy-one.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hard doctrine nobody understands.
what it means: one God in three persons, the answer Catholics trace on their bodies in the sign of the cross.
what a scholar hears: Tertullian's Latin trinitas around 200, the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople, and John XXII's extension of the feast in 1334.

672.title: Corpus Christi
672.hook: the Eucharist carried through the streets
672.howItsDone: On Corpus Christi, the Thursday after Trinity Sunday or, in many countries, the following Sunday, Catholic parishes celebrate the Eucharist and often hold a procession carrying the host in a monstrance through the streets, stopping at outdoor altars for Benediction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Trinity Sunday and the sign of the cross. Your line was one god, three persons. Did you slow it down? Day six hundred seventy-two.

In towns from Spain to the Philippines to Brooklyn, on one Sunday in early summer, traffic stops. Children in first-communion white scatter rose petals on the pavement. In some places the streets have been covered overnight in carpets of colored sawdust and flowers. A priest walks under a canopy carried on four poles, holding up a gold sunburst with a small white host at its center. Behind him, a brass band, a choir, families, the elderly with walkers. They stop at little altars set up on street corners. Today, the feast of that procession.
screen: `TRAFFIC STOPS.` → `PETALS AND SAWDUST CARPETS.` → `A GOLD SUNBURST UNDER A CANOPY.`

segments.voice: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread becomes Christ's body, truly present, and they already celebrate that every Holy Thursday. But Holy Thursday is crowded with the passion. So in the 1200s a nun in Belgium, Juliana of Liège, pressed for a feast of its own, with nothing else in the way. In 1264 Pope Urban IV established it for the whole Church, and tradition says he asked Thomas Aquinas to write the prayers and hymns. Some of the best known Latin hymns come from that work: Pange lingua, with its last verses, Tantum ergo, still sung at Benediction, and the long sequence Lauda Sion. The Gospel for the feast in one year is John six, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." The gold sunburst is called a monstrance, from the Latin monstrare, to show. The whole point is showing. The host isn't kept in the tabernacle today. It's carried out of the church, past the bakery and the bus stop and the bar, through the places people actually live. Christians understand the Eucharist in different ways: some see it mainly as a memorial, while Catholics, Orthodox and a number of other churches speak of a real presence. For Catholics, today's procession says something simple: the Christ they receive at the altar belongs on the street too. And this ends week ninety-six: Divine Mercy, the Good Shepherd, Fatima, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Trinity, and now the body carried through town.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk and pray for your street. If you can, go outside and walk slowly, even just to the corner and back. If you can't, picture your street from your window. Pass each door in your mind: the family with the new baby, the house that's been quiet since someone died, the shop owner, the person you've never met. If you pray, you can pray for each one as you pass. If you don't, simply wish each household well. The bell holds the time.
Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: the feast of the Eucharist, established for the whole Church in 1264, kept with processions through the streets. Today's word.
Your line: carried through the streets. Today, on your way somewhere, carry one person on your street in your mind, and say their name. Day six hundred seventy-two.
